scenes.heading: What pH really measures
scenes.narration: Chemistry uses the pH scale to measure the concentration of tiny hydrogen ions floating freely in a liquid solution. More ions mean a stronger chemical activity happening right there.

scenes.heading: The middle point of seven
scenes.narration: The entire scale spans cleanly from 0 to 14. Exactly in the middle sits the neutral value 7, where solutions are neither too active nor harmful.

scenes.heading: Acids and bases defined
scenes.narration: Moving below 7 brings you to the acidic side, filled with sour reactivity. Going above 7 leads to the basic side, which feels soapy and caustic.

scenes.heading: How each step multiplies
scenes.narration: Every single step on this scale represents a massive logarithmic shift. Each jump means the concentration multiplies by ten times compared to the step before.

scenes.heading: Everyday chemicals in action
scenes.narration: You can anchor these ideas to real liquids. Lemon juice sits near 2, pure water rests at 7, and strong cleaning bleach reaches all the way to 13.
